8 ways to use Claude and Gemini 4 Neon together

Give each model a role, define what it hands over, and decide how you’ll check the handoff.

An illustrated tutorial based on Mark Kashef’s YouTube walkthrough

Why the same job can produce different behavior

Kashef compares system prompts, the instructions supplied by an agent’s runtime before you enter your task, from Claude Code and Google’s Antigravity command-line interface. In the versions he examined, Neon is steered toward asking before assuming, batching tool calls, and coordinating agents. The Claude prompts he examined emphasize exercising judgment once enough information is available. He singles out Fable for continuing through routine errors.

Those observations come from the prompts he inspected. Model training and the surrounding software both influence what an agent does. The workflows below use the differences Kashef describes to decide who plans, who produces the work, and who checks it.

Captions 0:18–1:52

1. The Committee

Claude leads → Neon agents review from distinct perspectives → Claude synthesizes

Kashef imagines giving Claude his agency website repository and asking it to coordinate Neon subagents with distinct visitor personas. A skeptical first-time visitor might question what the agency does or whether to trust it. A returning visitor can evaluate whether the page answers enough questions to book a call. Claude collects their observations into a review of the visitor journey.

Kashef names MiroFish as an optional tool for simulating larger groups and suggests collecting representative lines from the simulated reviewers. Treat those lines as hypotheses about where real visitors could get stuck. Mark them as simulated if you share the synthesis. The same structure can review a client presentation or a draft community post.

Captions 1:54–3:15

2. Get independent opinions

Identical brief → Opus and Neon work in separate threads → compare evidence

Give both models the same meeting notes, interviews, and decision constraints. Keep their responses private from each other until each has made a recommendation. Kashef’s example asks each model to choose one of two candidate features from five customer interviews and identify the exact interview line that tipped its decision.

Compare the evidence as well as the choices. Agreement based on different interview evidence gives you a different reason for confidence than agreement based on rereading the same ambiguous line. If they disagree, look for the assumption or customer need that changes the priority.

Captions 3:14–4:09

Run both models in one workspace

Kashef mentions T3 Code and Orca as interfaces for running agent sessions side by side and passing project files or tasks between them. Separate threads support independent reviews. Shared files support explicit handoffs. Two separate chats and a shared specification file are enough to try the manual version.

Captions 4:10–4:43 · Kashef’s workflow kit

3. Plan, then build

Fable designs and scopes → you review the specification → Neon implements and tests

For a drag-and-drop project board, have Fable define the data model, valid stage changes, and edge cases before anyone writes code. Review the plan with Fable and remove scope you don’t need. Then send the final specification to Neon to build and test the front end. Kashef also suggests letting Neon review the plan or switching models between phases where the work changes.

Make the specification precise enough to build from. For example, define the expected result when a card is dropped into a new column and saving the update fails. That gives Neon a behavior to implement and a test to run.

Captions 4:44–5:56

4. Build two pieces in parallel

Shared clip-time format → Neon builds the editing timeline while Sonnet builds the exporter

In Kashef’s video-clipping tool example, Neon owns the interface folder and builds the timeline. Sonnet owns the scripts that cut and export the clip. Both use the same definition of the start and end times. That lets each work independently while preserving a clear integration point.

For an actual build, settle units and rounding before either starts. Then take one selection from the timeline and verify that the exported video starts and ends where the interface indicated. Passing that check verifies the handoff between the two pieces.

Captions 5:57–6:37

5. Pick the model by the input

Neon reads the footage + Opus or Sonnet analyzes the transcript and comments → combine by timestamp

To break down a YouTube video or an ad, Kashef sends the actual video to Neon for visual changes, cuts, pacing, and energy. He has Opus or Sonnet examine the transcript and comments to understand what the script says and what viewers reacted to. His example starts with a timed log of the first 60 seconds, then brings those observations together into a blueprint for the next video.

Use timestamps to align the script and visuals. Comments can add evidence about what viewers noticed. A comment praising a reveal, for example, can point you to a moment worth studying without establishing what caused the reaction.

Captions 7:13–7:58

6. Run a repair loop

Neon finds the visual bug → Opus patches the code → Neon repeats the same check

The example is a mobile checkout page whose total becomes almost invisible in dark mode even though its code tests pass. Ask Neon to capture the page in light and dark mode at the same mobile width. Send Opus the visual failure and where to reproduce it, then give Neon the updated page and the original test conditions.

Kashef caps the loop at three tries and suggests a precise success rubric. Here the acceptance check can be as direct as verifying that the order total is readable in both themes at the tested width. Keep before-and-after screenshots so the recheck is easy to inspect.

Captions 7:59–9:02

7. Let the lead agent delegate

Neon owns the deliverable → Claude handles bounded jobs → Neon integrates the results

Kashef reverses the lead role from the Committee. For a 3D studio mockup, Neon works from room photos and decides when it needs help. In his example prompt, Sonnet handles furniture sizing and the budget breakdown, and Opus researches options. Neon uses their results to update the room layout.

The division works when the delegated tasks have clear outputs. For the studio, ask for dimensions with units and budget estimates with sources or assumptions. A physical measurement can resolve uncertain dimensions before the layout treats them as fixed.

Captions 9:02–9:57

8. Use both models as release gatekeepers

Opus and Neon check the release independently → both must pass before it goes live

Give both models the finished release and a common checklist. Kashef suggests starting Neon on the front end and Opus on the back end, then having them swap. Both review areas such as links, permissions, and the complete user journey, including whether front-end actions work against the back end.

Any blocking failure pauses release. In Kashef’s illustration, the Continue button fails during setup, so the release stays on hold. The repair loop can address the issue first, then both checks can run again on the updated release. The two flows serve different decisions. The repair loop checks one fix. The gatekeeper checks whether a specific version is ready to ship.

Captions 9:57–11:00

What’s Next

Try the repair loop on one page you already maintain. Run it once with a single model and once with Neon inspecting and Opus fixing. Start both runs on the same revision, use the same visual acceptance check, and compare time to verified fix, attempts, and whether an independent recheck catches anything new. That gives you a way to measure the value of the second model in your own setup.
